title: Google and Blackstone Are Building a $5-Billion TPU Cloud Company. India's AI Ambitions Just Got a New Power Source.
excerpt: The joint venture — 500 megawatts of AI compute by 2027, led by a 20-year Google infrastructure veteran — creates the first major alternative to renting GPUs from hyperscalers, with direct implications for India's booming AI startup ecosystem.
body:
Google and Blackstone announced on May 18 that they are creating a new U.S.-based company dedicated to selling Google Cloud's Tensor Processing Units as a compute-as-a-service offering. Blackstone, the world's largest alternative asset manager with over $1.3 trillion in assets, is committing an initial $5 billion in equity. The venture expects to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by 2027, with plans to scale significantly after that.

**What This Actually Is**

The new company will own and operate data centres equipped with Google's custom-designed TPU chips — the same silicon that powers Gemini, Google Search's AI features, and workloads for many of the world's top AI labs and financial firms. Customers will be able to rent TPU compute directly from this entity, bypassing the need to go through Google Cloud.

Think of it as the AI equivalent of an independent power producer: Blackstone builds and finances the infrastructure, Google supplies the hardware and software, and customers get another option beyond the three hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) that currently dominate AI compute.

Benjamin Treynor Sloss, a Google executive with over two decades of experience building the company's global infrastructure, has been named CEO. His appointment signals that this is not a paper partnership — Google is lending serious operational talent.

**Why It Matters for Indian Tech**

India's AI ecosystem is growing at breakneck speed. The government's IndiaAI Mission, NITI Aayog's projections of AI adding up to $600 billion to GDP by 2035, and a surge in AI startup funding have all created one bottleneck: compute. Indian AI startups, research labs, and enterprises struggle to secure affordable GPU and TPU capacity. Most rely on Google Cloud, AWS, or Azure credits that are expensive, rationed, and subject to the whims of Big Tech's pricing teams.

A dedicated TPU cloud company, separate from Google Cloud, could offer Indian customers more flexible pricing, dedicated capacity contracts, and the ability to negotiate directly with an infrastructure-focused entity rather than a cloud platform with a thousand other priorities.

The Indian diaspora angle is equally significant. Thousands of Indian-origin engineers work in Google's TPU and infrastructure divisions. Sundar Pichai's Google has been the most visible champion of custom AI silicon, and this venture effectively takes that advantage and makes it available outside Google's walled garden.

**The Nvidia Question**

The deal is also a strategic shot across Nvidia's bow. Jensen Huang's company dominates AI compute through its H100 and Blackwell GPUs, and its market capitalisation has soared past $3 trillion on the back of that monopoly. Google's TPUs are the most credible alternative — they've been in production for over a decade and are optimised specifically for AI training and inference.

By creating a standalone company with Blackstone's capital, Google is signalling that TPUs can compete for the same enterprise customers that currently default to Nvidia GPUs. If the venture succeeds, it could reshape AI infrastructure economics globally.

**The Bigger Picture**

Big Tech's capital expenditure on AI infrastructure hit $130 billion in Q1 2026 alone. Google has separately committed $40 billion to Anthropic and is building its most powerful supercomputers to date. The Blackstone venture fits into a broader pattern: the AI industry is moving from a model where compute is a cloud service to one where compute is an infrastructure asset class, financed and operated like power plants or data pipelines.

For India — both the country and its diaspora — the implications are practical. More TPU capacity, available outside Google Cloud's standard pricing, means more runway for Indian AI startups, cheaper inference costs for the Indian enterprises building AI products, and a new career pathway for the Indian engineers who will build and operate these facilities.

Jon Gray, Blackstone's president, called it "a generational opportunity." For India's AI ambitions, it might be exactly that.
